overview: “Mandes” is a broad map label for diverse Mande-speaking peoples, not one kingdom. Its enormous 900 to 1000 polygon should not be read as a precise language frontier. Regional archaeology and clearly dated later examples reveal distinct communities, occupations and artistic traditions; they do not give every enclosed settlement one identity.

sections.title: Many communities and an early urban world

items.text: Mande is a language family with dozens of members, divided into major Western and South-Eastern branches. Sharing linguistic relationships does not make their speakers one dynasty, religion or occupation. The map’s short label covers a far more varied human story.

At Jenné-jeno in Mali, excavators traced a city that had grown to roughly thirty-three hectares by about 600 to 800 CE. Its substantial mud-brick enclosure and neighboring settlement mounds show urban life before the Mali Empire. This is regional evidence, not a census of its residents’ languages.

The 1977 excavations at Jenné-jeno recovered evidence of African rice, fish and cattle. These linked floodplain farming, fishing and herding in an economy that supported permanent settlement. A city’s history can begin with reliable meals as well as famous rulers.

Sandstone grinding equipment and volcanic stone ornaments found in the delta had to come from beyond the local floodplain. The excavators also identified distant copper and gold connections during the first millennium CE. Everyday food preparation and personal decoration both depended on exchange.

sections.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues

items.text: Later excavations at Jenné-jeno found relatively little variation between sampled areas in quantities of imported copper, stone and other goods. That complicates an easy picture of one fabulously rich quarter. The researchers caution that vanished materials, including textiles, could once have displayed differences that no longer survive.

At nearby Djenné, a different, later excavation uncovered a well lined with stacked pots whose bottoms were open. Lower occupation deposits were provisionally dated to the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries. Ceramic vessels could serve underground engineering as well as kitchens.

A photograph taken in Sissingué in 1992 records potter Fatoumata Kouyaté beginning a vessel with a cylinder of clay. She presses and hollows it by hand, then draws the sides upward. This named craftswoman’s method makes the shaping process visible, before firing turns soft clay into a useful container.

A Malinke hunter’s shirt in the Carlos Museum, made in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, carries leather packets, shells, claws and horns on cloth. Its attachments expressed accumulated knowledge and protective beliefs. The garment could become a changing record of its wearer’s experience.

sections.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample

items.text: At Nyagassola in Guinea, the Dökala family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a balafon associated with Manding epic traditions. Its twenty wooden slats have calabashes beneath them. UNESCO’s account describes a living musical responsibility passed within a family, not simply an old object in storage.

The Balatigui, the instrument’s guardian, also teaches balafon to children from about seven years old. UNESCO identified the departure of young people from the village as a threat to transmission. An instrument’s future depends on someone learning how to play it.

A 2004 N’Ko encoding proposal prints “ߕߐ߮”, transliterated tô and translated “name”. It explains that related Manding varieties can share this spelling while pronouncing it differently. This is an attested modern written example; N’Ko was devised in 1949, long after the map’s medieval interval.

N’Ko records vowels and tone with letters and added marks. Its decorative sign “߷”, called gbakurunen, represents the three stones that hold a cooking pot over a fire and marks major text divisions. A familiar household arrangement thus has a place on the written page.

ending.text: The map’s endpoint in 1000 is not the fall of the Mande-speaking peoples. Different communities subsequently joined or formed states, changed livelihoods and developed new forms of writing and art. Their shared language relationships never gave them one founding date or a single ending.
